subject: maths
chapter_title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

concepts.title: The Cartesian Coordinate System
concepts.definition: A reference frame for the flat plane, built from one horizontal number line (the x-axis) and one vertical number line (the y-axis), held at 90 degrees from one another. Every location gets fixed by an ordered pair of numbers, one taken from each line.
concepts.key_idea: Two number lines crossed at 90 degrees give every point in the plane an address.
question_patterns: Explain how the two coordinate axes are used to describe positions in a plane.
Define the x-axis and the y-axis in your own words.
Draw and label the parts of the coordinate plane, including both axes.
What makes the two axes of a coordinate frame perpendicular to each other?
State why a single number line is not enough to fix a position on a flat sheet.

solution_steps.explain: The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis.
Each location in the plane is named by one number from each axis.
The two axes meet at 90 degrees, which is what allows every point to have a unique ordered-pair address.

concepts.title: The Origin
concepts.definition: Both axes meet in one special spot labelled O. It acts as the zero mark for each axis, and its ordered pair has zero in both positions.
concepts.key_idea: Counting starts here; both entries of this ordered pair are zero.
question_patterns: What are the coordinates of the origin?
Locate and mark the origin on a graph paper grid.
Why is the spot where the two axes cross a good place to start counting?
Identify the ordered pair that represents the point where both axes meet.
State the distance of the origin from each of the two axes.

solution_steps.explain: The origin is the point (0,0) where the axes intersect.
Since O is the zero mark for each axis, its ordered pair has zero in both positions.
The origin is zero units from both the x-axis and the y-axis, making it the natural starting point for counting.

compute_steps.explain: apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dx = 10 - 1 gives 9
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dy = 14 - 2 gives 12
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dist = sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy) gives 15

concepts.title: Coordinates of a Point
concepts.definition: A location P is written as an ordered pair (x, y). Entry one gives the sideways gap of P to the y-axis; entry two gives the up-or-down gap of P to the x-axis.
concepts.formula: P = (x, y); x = gap from y-axis, y = gap from x-axis
concepts.key_idea: An address pair: sideways offset first, then up-or-down offset.
question_patterns: Read off the coordinates of a point marked on a grid.
For the point (6, -2), state how far it sits from each of the two axes.
Explain what the two entries of an ordered pair (x, y) tell you about a point.
If a point sits 4 units from the y-axis and 3 units from the x-axis, write its coordinates.
Distinguish between the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate of a marked point.

solution_steps.explain: The first number is the sideways offset from the vertical axis.
The second number is the vertical offset from the horizontal axis.
Writing the two entries as (x, y) gives the complete address of the point, with the sideways offset first and the up-or-down offset second.

concepts.title: Quadrants of the Plane
concepts.definition: The two axes split the whole flat surface into four open regions; numbering them I through IV starts at the top-right region and runs anticlockwise.
concepts.key_idea: Sign pattern of the ordered pair picks the region: (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-).
question_patterns: In which quadrant does the point (-3, 5) lie?
Name the quadrant containing a point whose x-entry is positive and y-entry is negative.
Which quadrant holds points with both entries negative?
Predict the quadrant of (7, -2) before plotting it.
List the sign pattern of the coordinates in each of the four regions.
Justify why no point can lie in two quadrants at once.

solution_steps.action: Check signs of x and y
solution_steps.explain: If x > 0 and y > 0, Quadrant I; if x < 0 and y > 0, Quadrant II; if x < 0 and y < 0, Quadrant III; if x > 0 and y < 0, Quadrant IV.
The four sign patterns (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-) correspond to quadrants I through IV, numbered starting from the top-right and going anticlockwise.
If either entry is zero, the point lies on an axis rather than inside any quadrant, so no quadrant assignment is made.

compute_steps.explain: apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dx = 16 - 7 gives 9
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dy = 4 - -8 gives 12
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dist = sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy) gives 15

concepts.title: Points on the Axes
concepts.definition: On the x-axis, every point has second entry zero; on the y-axis, every point has first entry zero.
concepts.key_idea: Points lying directly on the boundary lines of the quadrants.
question_patterns: What is the y-coordinate of any point on the x-axis?
Write the coordinates of a point 5 units to the left of the origin on the x-axis.
Where does the point (0, -4) lie?
Decide whether the point (7, 0) sits on the x-axis or the y-axis, and say why.
Give the general form of the coordinates of a point on the y-axis.

solution_steps.explain: If y is 0, the point is on the x-axis. If x is 0, the point is on the y-axis.
A point on the x-axis has the form (x, 0) and a point on the y-axis has the form (0, y), reflecting which coordinate is always zero.

solution_steps.action: Confirm the point is not in a quadrant
solution_steps.explain: Since one entry is zero, the point lies on a boundary line between quadrants rather than inside any single quadrant.

compute_steps.explain: apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dx = 24 - 4 gives 20
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dy = 13 - -8 gives 21
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dist = sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy) gives 29

concepts.title: Distance Between Two Points
concepts.definition: For a slanting segment, the length comes from the right-triangle result credited to Baudhayana: square each coordinate gap between the endpoints, add the squares, and take the square root.
concepts.key_idea: Treat the gap between the endpoints as the two legs of a right triangle; the segment is its hypotenuse.
question_patterns: Calculate the distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2).
Find the length of the segment joining A(3, 4) and D(7, 1).
Compute how far apart M(9, 6) and D(7, 1) are.
Use the right-triangle result to find a side length of a triangle drawn on a grid.
Check whether the segment between (-2, 3) and (1, 7) has integer length.

solution_steps.explain: Subtract the x-coordinates.
Subtract the y-coordinates.
Square the differences, sum them, and take the square root.

concepts.title: Midpoint of a Segment
concepts.definition: For endpoints S(x1, y1) and T(x2, y2), the halfway location M has entries that average each pair of matching endpoint entries.
concepts.key_idea: Each entry of the halfway point is the mean of the matching endpoint entries.
question_patterns: How do you test whether M is the midpoint of segment ST?
State the connection between the coordinates of S, T and their halfway point.
Given one endpoint S(3, -4) and the halfway point M(-7, 1), predict the other endpoint.
Explain why averaging the two x-entries gives the x-entry of the halfway point.
Use the midpoint idea to locate the centre of a segment on a grid.

solution_steps.explain: Add x1 and x2, then halve the sum.
Add y1 and y2, then halve the sum.
The two averages form the ordered pair M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2), which is the halfway point of the segment.

compute_steps.explain: apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dx = -2 - -7 gives 5
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dy = 18 - 6 gives 12
apply the coordinate-geometry formula: dist = sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy) gives 13

concepts.title: Distance between points on a line parallel to axes
concepts.definition: When two endpoints share their y-entry, subtract the x-entries and drop the sign; when they share their x-entry, do the same with the y-entries.
concepts.formula: same y: dist = abs(x2 - x1); same x: dist = abs(y2 - y1)
concepts.key_idea: Simplified distance calculation for horizontal or vertical segments.
question_patterns: Points P(3, 5) and Q(8, 5) share the same y-coordinate; find the distance PQ.
How far apart are (2, -1) and (2, 7), which sit on one vertical line?
Calculate the length of the horizontal segment joining A(0, -2) and M(-5, -2).
What is the length of side MP with M(-5, -2) and P(-5, 2)?
Without plotting, state which coordinate entries to compare when both points share the same y-value.

solution_steps.explain: If y1 = y2, use x-difference. If x1 = x2, use y-difference.
Subtract the matching coordinate entries and drop the sign, since length is always non-negative.
The absolute difference gives the length of the horizontal or vertical segment directly, with no need for the full distance formula.
